render.title: Krebs cycle electron carriers passed to the transport chain
render.body:
The TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle — also called the Krebs cycle — does not produce much ATP directly. Its main job is to strip high-energy electrons from organic molecules and load them onto carrier molecules that then deliver those electrons to the electron transport chain.

For each turn of the cycle (one acetyl-CoA processed), the Krebs cycle produces:

- 3 NADH: These carry electrons to Complex I (and in some cases Complex II) of the electron transport chain. NADH is the more energy-rich carrier; each NADH ultimately drives the pumping of roughly 10 protons across the inner membrane.
- 1 FADH2: This carrier donates electrons directly to Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). Because it enters the chain at a later step than NADH, each FADH2 drives pumping of fewer protons (roughly 6) and therefore yields less ATP.
- 1 GTP (or ATP, depending on the organism): This is made directly by substrate-level phosphorylation and is not passed to the transport chain — it is already a usable energy molecule.

Because one glucose molecule produces two acetyl-CoA molecules, a full pass through glycolysis and the Krebs cycle generates 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 from the cycle itself (plus 2 NADH from glycolysis). All of these are handed to the electron transport chain, where they drive proton pumping, build the proton gradient, and ultimately power ATP synthase to make the bulk of the cell's ATP.
render.summary: The Krebs cycle hands 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, and 1 GTP to downstream processes per acetyl-CoA. The NADH and FADH2 carry electrons into the electron transport chain, where they drive proton pumping and ATP synthesis.
